..
Issued at 337 AM CDT Tue Sep 22 2026

Weak mid to upper level flow over the Northern Plains early 
this morning, with a ridge over eastern Manitoba/western Ontario
and a trough approaching the Upper Mississippi River Valley. 
Meanwhile, low level to surface southerly return flow is 
increasing as a result of lee troughing along the slopes of the 
Northern Rockies and broad high pressure stretched across the 
northern Great Lakes. The southerly return flow has lead to an 
increase in low stratus across southern parts of the state. The 
low clouds may continue to expand through the morning and linger
in some areas through the afternoon, keeping high temperatures 
in the upper 50s to mid 60s. Wherever sunshine is more 
plentiful, upper 60s and lower 70s can be expected for highs 
this afternoon. South-southeast winds could increase to around 
20-25 mph with gusts as high as 35 mph this afternoon as the lee
trough shifts eastward while the downstream high remains in 
place. A persistent south-southeast breeze through tonight 
should keep low temperatures in the mid 40s to lower 50s.

The benign mid to upper level flow pattern will turn 
southwesterly on Wednesday with the arrival of a shortwave that 
is spinning over the Great Basin this morning. Chances for 
showers begin to increase in southwest North Dakota early 
Wednesday morning with the arrival of DCVA and underlying warm 
air advection, spreading northeastward through through the 
morning and into the afternoon. A few thunderstorms will be 
possible across central North Dakota in the afternoon, but model
soundings show convection should remain elevated with only up 
to around 500 J/kg MUCAPE and effective bulk shear 25 kts or 
less. Shower and thunderstorm chances diminish from west to east
during the afternoon and evening. However, there is a low 
chance for convective initiation along the lee surface trough in
western North Dakota late Wednesday afternoon. Any 
thunderstorms in this time and space would more likely be 
surface-based with up to 1000 J/kg CAPE and 30 kts deep layer 
shear, which could result in a stronger storm. Whether storms 
actually develop here remains highly uncertain though as low 
level warm air advection and the 700 mb trough may not be 
properly phased to provide stronger support for ascent.

Showers and associated cloudiness limit forecast highs to the 
60s in central and northwest North Dakota on Wednesday, with the
southwest warming into the lower and mid 70s. Behind the 
departure of the shortwave, upper level ridging is forecast to 
amplify on Thursday, warming forecast high temperatures back 
into the lower 70s east to lower 80s west. By Friday morning, a 
deeper trough is forecast to land on the Pacific Northwest while
a ridge axis remains in place over the Mississippi River 
Valley, briefly turning flow aloft northerly. A shortwave is 
forecast to lift off the Foothills of Colorado/Wyoming early 
Friday, bringing medium chances for rain across the state from 
south/southwest to north/northeast Friday through Friday night. 
Forecast QPF is light (ensemble mean around a few hundredths to 
a couple tenths of an inch), and there is little to no chance 
for a thunderstorm. Most locations are likely to see a slight 
cool down in high temperatures on Friday due to the increased 
shower chances and associated cloud cover. 

On Saturday, the deeper upstream trough is forecast to swing 
northeastward into the Canadian prairie region, picking up the 
shortwave responsible for Friday's rain chances. This could lead
to a warmer Saturday, but the southern Canadian trough could 
begin to drive a cold front through the region by Saturday 
afternoon. Ensembles tend to favor southwest flow through the 
weekend as a deep but progressive trough moves across the 
western CONUS. This trough is responsible for widespread medium 
rain chances in the forecast from Sunday night through Monday 
and into Tuesday. But there is considerable uncertainty in the 
evolution of this trough. One potential outcome is for the base 
of the trough to cut off from the northern stream, which would 
leave the Northern Plains under split flow with a much lower 
rain potential. Ensemble clusters show mean height fields to be 
broad and smooth late Sunday through Monday, making it difficult
to discern if one particular outcome is more probable than 
others. NBM temperature distributions do begin to shift cooler 
early next week, but remain close to late September averages.
